I've tried Dune three times now. I've never been able to make it more than about 50 pages deep. What am I missing? Do I just need to push through to get to better storyline?

First 50 pages are merely an introduction, to get you to start grasping the universe where the whole thing is taking place. Dune actually has a lot of action, which unfolds quickly, once the "intro" part is over, but you need to get to at least 60% of the book before you start to see amazing things.

I remember that when I was ~18 I struggled with Dune, and dropped it. Later started once again when I was 25, and in one month binge-reading episode I've finished the whole series (6 books, ~2-2.5k pages) during less than 1 month.

It's a pretty similar thing to what I remember from the Lord Of The Rings... first pages about Hobbiton, Bilbo, Bilbo's party is boring as hell, but serve a great purpose of introducing you to the completely alien universe. Unlike LOTR, though, I would advise you not to try to make sense of everything you read, not to memorize terms and characters - it's pointless and distracts you from bigger concepts. Dune universe is very strange (hell... sci-fi, space flight and interplanetary wars without computers, who'd think of that in any sci-fi?) so it's perfectly fine to not understand a lot of things. Later, either after rereading, or getting a "woah!" moment when thinking about during a shower, it'll start to fall into place.

Voat is currently talking to VCs about funding. Atko has mentioned patents in one of his previous posts (on what?). VC funding is the reason that Reddit is turning into a monstrosity. VCs are not angels, good samaritans, or altruistic idealists*. They are investors. They expect a return.

Victoria was fired because she (allegedly) didn't want to support monetizing /r/iama in the way Reddit (meaning Reddit's investors) want to.

KickMe444 was fired from his position at Reddit (after recovering from cancer), which was to manage redditgifts, one of the juiciest and easist monetization targets for investors.

The reddit backlash against free speech and push for "safe spaces" is most likely an attempt to homogenize reddit's community into a demographic more suited for ad traffic.

If Voat takes VC money, regardless of what Atko wants or what the community wants, eventually Voat will suffer the same fate as Reddit - investors seeking to make the most money out of a potential loss.

I understand that Voat is expensive to run, and growing quickly, but there has already been a vast outpouring of goodwill from our small but growing community. We've ignored server instability, outages, and DDoSes precisely because we do not want to be on Reddit.

If Voat accepts VC money, unless they somehow get some sort of ridiculous term sheet where they get buckets of cash at an astronomical valuation (basically a loan), they will eventually become Reddit. The purpose of Voat, long term, becomes about ROI rather than the community, and as we've seen from Reddit, Digg, Slashdot, Fark, etc, those two purposes are never aligned unless the community are the owners (MeFi, SA, etc).

Atko, I know you've poured a huge amount of your time, effort, and probably not an unsubstantial amount of money into Voat. Please work with the community on a deal to allow Voat to be run without investment. It's the only way that Voat can survive, long-term.

* VCs almost certainly capable of being good people, however their job is not to give away money, it is to make money for their clients.
Why is Voat seeking VC money when that is exactly the problem that Reddit is having right how?

Is there really another option? Practically, the site needs money to survive. Server space at the volume required is hardly cheap, I think until Bill Gates feels like privately funding something it's a necessary evil. I guess the only thing we can do is hope Voat can be better than Paoddit.

Server space is always cheap, relatively speaking. Compared to the servers (VPSes) themselves, storage is a drop in the proverbial bucket.

Edit: To more directly answer your question, I think it's pretty clear after 20 years of failures that a need to make money off of a community will always eventually taint that community, unless the exchange is direct.

I'm pretty ignorant to the details of hosting. But I think there are plenty of examples that show the monetization of a site are death bells. It sucks jumping between communities every 5 years or so, but what else is there to do?

User-monetized sites' biggest metrics are churn (which we'll ignore here) and ARPU, or average revenue per user. Generally, an ARPU of $5 for a site like Reddit or Voat is considered fantastic. Properly managed, it can cost Reddit less than a dollar per year to serve you. If every active user of Reddit gave $5 a year, their financials would be great. Alternately, if 50% of people give $10, 10% of people give $50, etc, same outlook. Many people will never give and some people can't.

A problem arises, though, when VCs have given Atko lets say $100,000 at a $5,000,000 valuation. That valuation assumes that Voat is going to make (in profit) close to $1,500,000 a year, and the investor is going to expect Voat to grow substantially. Even if Voat is making enough money to pay for Atko's time and a small team of staff just from donations (which is healthy), the VC is not going to be happy. She is going to want to see profit increase quickly as the userbase grows, and while it would be great for users of Voat was a small, healthy business, it would be awful for that investor, who would wind up seeing little return on their money.

This is not the VC being the bad guy, she is just doing her job, which is to make somewhat risky investments and make money for her investors, higher up the chain.

Yea, this is all way out of my wheelhouse so please forgive my ignorance. Didn't they show this relationship on the HBO show Silicon Valley? If that's the case, couldn't Voat just go with the lowest bidder and do it's best to curtail an initial over estimation of it's potential?

You generally get shat on in equity if your valuation is too low. The higher your valuation in your seed round, the more of your company you get to keep. Then, in your A, B, and (potentially) C round, you want to keep expectations tailored. If you have a $100m valuation in your A round, you cannot raise funding (snowball's chance in hell) at a $75m valuation for your B round. It's likely also impossible to raise again at $100m.
